And a true believer, who is certain that God is aware of all the secrets and hidden things of his breast, trembles at the thought that such and such thoughts are in his heart. Through this he cleanses his consciousness and feelings, and purifies his heart as well.

The truth is that as soon as faith arises, a moral beauty arises within man. He believes that there is a God who is just, merciful, generous and forgiving, forbearing and loving; He does not like evil, He likes good. He knows the treachery of the eyes and is the Knower of the secrets of hearts.

(7) Then there is the idea that man has been given freedom of will, and along with it complete watchfulness from God. As a result, a sense and awareness arise in a person, and through the understanding and reflection that arise, man regards himself as responsible, and he adopts a responsible attitude toward every good as its due, and also feels responsibility toward other human beings. This responsibility is before God. Therefore, when a believer does any deed, his feeling and consciousness is that he reflects in his heart on every matter and every step, and considers the consequences before taking the step. For according to this conception man is a creature who holds a position in this world, and so in the order of this universe he is a responsible creature.

(8) One of the important effects of faith is that a believer does not fall upon the benefits of this world as dogs fall upon bones. Among the signs and effects of faith is that he chooses that which has a lofty purpose in God's sight, which is "good" and which endures.

﴿...and for this let the competitors compete﴾ (83:26). "If the competitors wish to compete, let them compete in goodness." Competition for the rewards that are with God raises man above this world, purifies his heart, and man becomes clean and pure. It also widens the sphere of a believer's activity. He goes beyond the borders of the world and is active in the Hereafter as well. Along with the earth he ranges in the higher world too, and this is what creates in him the strength to go on doing good without regard for the results, or without haste about the results. For he wants goodness because it is goodness and because it is God's will so; it is not his responsibility that the results of goodness should appear within this short, limited life. For the God for whom this good is done is Living and does not die. He does not forget, and is not heedless of anything. Moreover, this world is not the true abode of recompense, and all accounts are not to be settled in this world. So the believer draws help, in order to continue doing good, from the source that never dries up, and this is why the movement of good continues. It is not a momentary enthusiasm, nor an individual occurrence. It is this spirit of faith that creates in a believer such strength that he stands up against the greatest evil, whether this evil takes the form of a dictator and tyrant, or of the pressure of jahili concepts and priorities, or of the desires of man's own self. This individual pressure falls upon a person in such a way that he thinks this world is short, life is brief, and one ought to enjoy pleasure and luxury in it:

"Babur, enjoy yourself, for the world will not come again."

Or it is so short that the results of good cannot appear in it, and for us there seems no chance to see the truth triumph over falsehood. Faith therefore treats this situation, and treats it fundamentally.

The truth is that faith is the foundation of life, the root of life; from it all the branches of goodness sprout, and every fruit hangs from these very roots. If there is no faith, it is as though the root of the tree has been cut, and all its branches will wither and dry up; and if they do not dry up, then it will be a satanic fruit, and it will not gain permanence or growth.

The truth is that faith is the centre and axis to which all the strings of higher life are tied, and if there is no faith, life is an unconnected motion, and without faith this life has no stability or rest. Wherever desires and inclinations go, they drag one along.

Faith is in reality a system, and through it all scattered deeds become linked with one another, and through it these deeds become harmonious with one another. They come to be in one direction, having one movement, one motive and one goal.

This is why the Noble Qur'an declares null and void every deed that is not based on this foundation, that does not revolve around this axis, and that does not spring from the source of faith. The Islamic view of life and the Islamic system of beliefs are completely open and explicit in this matter. In Surah Ibrahim it says:

﴿The example of those who disbelieved in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows violently on a stormy day. They have no power over anything of what they earned﴾ (14:18). And in Surah an-Nur it says:

﴿And those who disbelieved, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty one thinks to be water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ (24:39). These texts state explicitly that as long as deeds are not based on faith, they have no worth in Islam. The feeling underlying deeds must be that the Creator of the universe has commanded this, and their aim must be to be in harmony with the purpose of this universe's creation. This is the logical outcome of the belief that returns all matters to God; therefore a deed whose connection with faith has been severed has lost its meaning and value. (Ustadh Muhammad 'Abduh, under the verse ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ (99:7–8), wrote: "Some scholars have recorded ijma' (consensus) that no good deed of a disbeliever will benefit him on the Day of Resurrection and that there will be no lightening of his punishment, but this is a fundamental point." We consider that this matter is not one of ijma' but of the explicit texts of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an and Sunnah are completely clear in this matter. (Sayyid Qutb))

Faith is proof that the believer's nature is sound and the makeup of his personality is whole, and that he walks in step with this entire universe. He is in harmony with the nature of the universe found all around him, and so he lives in this universe at home. When a believer's personality is sound, there is a concord between him and this universe, and this concord and unity is only the fruit of faith. For in this universe there are proofs and signs which show that there is one Hand of Power, the Maker of the universe. So if this concord between man and the universe disappears, that is proof that his personality has been damaged and that the faculty by which he draws proofs and signs from this universe has died. Because of this corruption, man will be in loss. Even if some deeds appear outwardly to bear the stamp of goodness, they will not be accepted for lack of faith.... In sum, the world of the believer is wide, comprehensive, long, high, beautiful and successful. By contrast, the world of those who do not believe is small, mean, fallen, weak, frustrated and made up of wretchedness, and its outcome and end is loss and frustration.

﴿وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ﴾ (103:3) "and did righteous deeds." Righteous action is in truth the natural fruit of faith. When faith settles in a heart, righteous action is its own inherent movement (just as the heart is in motion). Faith is therefore a living and positive movement: as soon as it settles in a personality, it appears in the form of righteous action. From the Islamic point of view, this is what faith is. Islam has no concept of a faith that is extinguished and produces no movement, that is hidden and does not emerge in living form from the believer's person. If it has no natural movement of this kind, it is a counterfeit and dead faith. Faith is a flower whose fragrance cannot be held back. Wherever there is a flower, fragrance will keep coming from it. And if a person has no scent of faith, it is as though it does not exist in him at all.

From this we learn that faith is a name for movement, action and construction, and that all of these are directed toward God. There is no contraction in faith, nor is it something negative, nor does it lie buried in the folds of the conscience. Nor is faith a matter of good wishes with no movement behind them. This is the open character of Islam, which makes Islam a lofty, constructive being, and this force is the central driving power within practical life.

This is the meaning of saying that faith must be connected with the Islamic system of life. The Islamic system of life is a continuous movement that runs through this entire universe; this movement was produced by a directing power, and it has a goal. To place the leadership of humanity in the hands of faith means to bring into being a leadership that produces a method of movement in accord with the character of this whole universe. In other words, it means to establish a good, pure, constructive striving worthy of the system of life that has come from God.

﴿وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ﴾ (103:3) "and enjoined one another to the truth, and enjoined one another to patience." In the acts of enjoining truth and enjoining patience, the features of the Muslim community (ummah) become clearly visible. The Muslim body (jama'ah) is also established on the lines of the Muslim ummah. It has a distinct existence and personality. Among its members there is a distinctive bond. All of them face one direction. This ummah or community is aware of its own existence, and keeps its duties before it. It knows what it has to do in relation to faith and righteous action, and it knows that, from the standpoint of faith and righteous action, it must lead all humanity. So to enjoin one another to the truth means: you are to rise bearing the greatest trust.

In sum, from the word "tawasi" (mutual enjoining), from its meaning, its character and its reality, the existence of the Muslim ummah emerges, or the idea of a mutually united community appears: an ummah that is distinguished, wise, and responsible for establishing truth, goodness and justice on this earth. This is a most lofty and beautiful picture of the Muslim ummah. Islam wants an ummah of this kind: distinguished, strong, wise, and a guardian of truth and goodness, whose members at all times counsel one another to the truth and enjoin patience, live with mutual love and cooperation, and between whom there is a special brotherhood, which the Qur'an expresses as "wasiyyah" (enjoining, bequest).

Enjoining the truth is necessary because carrying the truth is a difficult task. In this world there are countless factors that lead a person away from the path of truth: carnal desires, expediencies, notions of nation and family, the oppression of tyrants and dictators, the wrongdoing of oppressors, the transgressions and excesses of those who overstep the limits, and so on. Counseling one another in fact serves as a reminder. A person's resolve grows, and unity and oneness arise among the members of the community in their aims and purposes. In bearing responsibilities, they in fact carry one another's burden. Through counsel all individual inclinations are gathered together and multiplied, and all those who guard and support the truth feel: "I am not alone. In the work of protecting truth and righteousness there are others with me, who counsel me, encourage me, love me, and stand behind me. They will never let me be put to shame." This religion is itself the truth, and only a community can protect this religion: one whose members know one another, vouch for one another, help one another, and make up for one another's weaknesses.

Enjoining patience is also very necessary, because to keep on in faith and righteous action and to guard truth and justice is a hard task. It calls for patience, steadfastness, and a severe struggle (jihad) against the factors within the self, and also a struggle against the factors outside the self, and it calls for patience and toil in the difficulties met on this path. Likewise: patience with the arrogance and boasting of falsehood, patience with the length of the road, patience with the slowness of success, and patience with the absence and fading of the road's landmarks.

Enjoining patience increases human strength, and creates among people a collective feeling that the goal of all of us is one and our direction is one; in this way everyone gains a support from it. Workers on this path become closely united as they labor, and advance with great resolve, firmness and insistence on their purpose. It also produces several other collective qualities, which are necessary for the strength of an Islamic community, because Islam cannot live without a communal atmosphere. Islam also appears in the form of a society. If there is no society at all, there will be no Islam, and that would be sheer loss.

The constitution that the Qur'an has laid down for us, according to which it declares a society successful and safe from loss in this world and the next: if we put on the spectacles of this constitution and survey the condition of the world at present, a frightening picture of the world appears before us, that the whole world is at present caught in complete loss. The more frightening aspect of this loss is that, even before the Hereafter, we have already fallen into severe loss from a purely worldly point of view. We see that humanity has turned away completely from the good whose blessings and bounties God had made general for mankind. Moreover, the supreme authority that is of faith and of Islam, and stands on the principles of goodness, truth and justice, has vanished from this world. The ugliest aspect of this picture is that the Muslims, or more correctly those people who, compared with the other human beings dwelling on this earth, have strayed far from this good and virtue, have gone far from the system of life which God had chosen for them. They have trampled the charter and constitution that God had prescribed for them, which God had declared the only way to be saved from loss and failure. In particular, the regions from which the banners of this good were first raised have themselves brought down the banners which God had raised for them. These were the banners of faith. And the great misfortune is that the regions from which these banners of God's religion were raised have adopted racial nationalism, although the history of this earth bears witness that no people has ever reached goodness through racial nationalism. The racial nationalism (Arab nationalism) whose banners these people have raised, they possessed even before Islam, but because of it they accomplished no notable deed on this earth, and no deed of theirs was recorded in heaven. When Islam came, through the Arabs it raised a banner that was God's alone, with no other element sharing in it; it was in God's name, with no partner even in the name; it was attributed only to God, with no other attribution; it bore only God's color, with no other color. Under this banner the Arabs rose to eminence. They became the leaders of the world. Their leadership was a leadership of goodness: a strong leadership, a wise leadership, and a leadership successful in every respect. This leadership succeeded for the first time in the history of the Arabs, and in human history the Islamic revolution was a conspicuous success for humanity.

Maulana Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi says in his famous book "The Effect of the Rise and Decline of Muslims on the Human World," in the chapter "Islamic Rule and Muslim Leaders":

"The Muslims came into the field, took the reins of the world's guidance into their own hands, and removed those sick nations from the position of leadership which they had seized and which they had never used properly. The Muslims took the people of the whole world with them and began to advance them at a balanced and proper pace toward their true destination. In them were gathered all the qualities that proved them fit for the exalted office of guiding all nations, and that guaranteed the welfare and happiness of the nations under their supervision and leadership. What were these distinguishing qualities? They are as follows:

(1) They had a heavenly Book and the law of God. They did not legislate or make law on their own, because human legislation is a source of ignorance, injustice and errors, and when human beings make laws for human beings, they are altered and amended every day, whereas the heavenly Books are safe from these errors. In their daily affairs, in politics and leadership, the Muslims were safe from walking blindly and groping in the dark. They had the light of divine revelation by which they walked, and by which all the paths and turns of life were lit for them. Every step of theirs fell in light, and they saw their destination clearly. In Surat al-An'am (122) it says:

﴿أَوَمَن كَانَ مَيْتًا فَأَحْيَيْنَاهُ وَجَعَلْنَا لَهُ نُورًا يَمْشِي بِهِ فِي النَّاسِ كَمَن مَّثَلُهُ فِي الظُّلُمَاتِ لَيْسَ بِخَارِجٍ مِّنْهَا﴾ (6:122) "Is he who was dead, then We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among people, like one who is in darkness from which he cannot emerge?"

They had a divine law and shari'ah by which they judged between people. They were made standard-bearers of truth and justice, and even in the severest state of provocation, anger, enmity and hatred they were commanded not to abandon truth and justice, and not to take revenge in matters of truth and justice.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ لِلَّهِ شُهَدَاءَ بِالْقِسْطِ وَلَا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ عَلَىٰ أَلَّا تَعْدِلُوا اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (5:8) "O you who believe, be steadfast for God, witnesses in justice, and let not the hatred of a people lead you to abandon justice. Be just; that is nearer to piety. And fear God; indeed God is aware of what you do."

(2) They came to the office of government and leadership after firm moral training and purification of the self. They did not leap from lowliness to eminence with all their moral faults and defects, like the ordinary ruling nations and rulers of the world. Rather, for a long period divine revelation kept reforming and training them, and for years they remained under the complete supervision and teaching of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He kept purifying them and trained them fully. He made them accustomed to a life of asceticism and scrupulousness, and habituated them to chastity, trustworthiness, selflessness, sacrifice and fear of God. He removed completely from their hearts the greed and craving for rule and office. His saying was: 'By God, we will not entrust any office to one who asked for it or who desires it.' Their hearts were wholly cleansed of the desire for exaltation, high rank and honor, and of the wish for strife and corruption. Night and day these words of the Qur'an fell on their ears:

﴿تِلْكَ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ نَجْعَلُهَا لِلَّذِينَ لَا يُرِيدُونَ عُلُوًّا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فَسَادًا وَالْعَاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ (28:83) "That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who do not desire exaltation upon the earth or corruption. And the best outcome is for the righteous.""

Therefore they did not fall upon government offices and posts in a rush; on the contrary, they shied away from accepting them, and trembled when they thought of their responsibilities. Whichever of them was offered a post would draw back and consider himself unfit for the burden, let alone that any of them would put forward his own name for government, or campaign on his own behalf. Then, when they took any responsibility into their hands, they did not regard it as war booty or an easy morsel; rather they regarded it as a trust (amanah) placed upon them and a trial from Allah. They were certain that they would have to appear before Allah and answer for everything, small and great. And they always recited this verse:
﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾ (4:58). And also this saying:
﴿And it is He who has made you successors (khulafa') on the earth and raised some of you above others in rank, that He may try you in what He has given you. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (6:165).

(3) They were not servants of any people, nor representatives of any race or homeland, whose sole concern would be the prosperity of that people and race, nor did they believe in the superiority of any people and in securing for it the position of leadership and mastery over all nations, holding the belief that "our nation exists to lead, and the other nations exist only to be ruled." They did not go out beyond the borders of the Arab world in order to establish an Arab empire over the world, to live a life of comfort and luxury under its shade, and to boast and act arrogantly over others under its protection. Nor did they go out to take people out of the slavery of the Romans and Persians and bring them into the slavery of the Arabs and themselves. They went out only to take the servants of God out of servitude to people like themselves and bring them into the servitude of Allah alone, who has no partner. The envoy of the Muslims, Rib'i ibn 'Amir, proclaimed this truth in the packed court of the Persian king Yazdgird. He said: "Allah has sent us to take people out of the worship of servants to the worship of the One Allah, from the narrowness of this world to the vastness of Allah's expanse, and from the oppression and tyranny of religions to the justice and fairness of Islam." So all the nations and all human beings of the world stood, in their eyes, in one position; if there was any difference, it was only a difference of religion. In short, they fully acted upon this saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "All people are Adam, and Adam is from clay. An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, except through taqwa (God-consciousness)."

And in Surat al-Hujurat, verse 13:
﴿O people, We created you from a male and a female, and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may know one another. Indeed, the most honoured of you in the sight of Allah is the one who is most God-conscious﴾ (49:13).

The son of 'Amr ibn al-'As, the governor of Egypt, once struck an Egyptian with a whip and boasted of his forefathers. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) ordered that the Egyptian take retribution from him, and said to 'Amr ibn al-'As: "Since when have you enslaved people, when their mothers bore them free?"

These conquerors and rulers never showed miserliness or narrow-mindedness in bestowing religion, knowledge and civilization, and in matters of government and its offices they never took account of nationality, color or race. They were a generous cloud that enveloped the whole world, whose bounty was general for all, which watered the whole world as it went, for which every part of the earth offered prayers, and from which creatures benefited according to their own capacity and ability.

Under the shade and rule of these people, all the nations of the world, regardless of differences of color, homeland and religion, had full opportunity to take their full share in knowledge, civilization and government, and to join the Arabs in the work of rebuilding. Indeed, many of their individuals surpassed the Arabs in many virtues, and among them arose imams, jurists (fuqaha') and hadith scholars (muhaddithin) who were a crown on the heads of the Arabs themselves and a source of pride for the Muslims.

(4) Man is a combination of body, heart and intellect. Man cannot attain true success and happiness, and humanity cannot be granted balanced progress, until all these faculties of his are developed and nurtured proportionately, in a manner befitting his rank. A righteous civilization cannot come into existence in the world until a religious, moral, intellectual and material environment is established in which it is possible for man to reach perfection with full ease. Experience has proven that this is not possible unless the guidance of life and the steering of civilization are in the hands of people who believe in both the spiritual and the material, who are a perfect model of religious and moral life, and who are characterized by sound intellect and correct knowledge. (pp. 100-164).

And in another chapter, under the heading "The Era of the Rightly-Guided Caliphate," he writes:

"Thus we know of no era in history more complete and successful in all these respects than the era of the Rightly-Guided Caliphate. In this era, spiritual, moral, religious and intellectual resources and means helped one another in bringing into existence the perfect human being and a righteous civilization. In this state, which was counted among the greatest states of the world, exalted moral models and high standards were at work alongside a political and material power that surpassed all contemporary powers. Along with trade and industry, morality and virtue were also at their full height. With the expansion of conquests and the progress of civilization, the progress of both morality and usefulness continued. Thus, despite the extraordinary expanse of the Islamic state, the extreme growth of population, and the means and temptations of luxury and comfort, crimes and incidents of immorality were very rare. The relationship of one individual with another, and of the individual with the community, was astonishing. It was an exemplary era of which the man of a more advanced age could not even dream, and no more blessed and flourishing time can even be imagined." (p. 167)

These were some features of that blessed era in which humanity, for a short period, lived under the Islamic constitution laid down by Surat al-'Asr. In that period people were ruled by a believing community of such people who had raised the banners of faith, whose program was righteous action, and whose hallmark was counseling to truth and urging to patience.

It was a golden age that can never be compared with the ruin that all of humanity faces today. In the battle between good and evil, all humanity is sunk in loss and destruction. All humanity has shut its eyes to that great good, when the Arabs were the leaders and guides of all humanity; and in the later periods, when they threw down these banners, they became servants of the caravan of humanity, while this caravan too is advancing toward the destination of ruin, and in the end the state has come to this: all humanity has taken up satanic banners, and none of them is a human banner. All humanity has taken up the banners of falsehood; nowhere is any banner of truth to be seen. All humanity has taken up the banners of blindness and misguidance; nowhere among them is a single banner of guidance and light to be seen. All the banners are banners of loss; not a single banner of success is to be seen. The banner of Allah, by means of which the Arabs overspread the world, still exists today. This banner still awaits a hand to raise it. There is need of a community or a people who would walk under this banner on the path of goodness, guidance, righteousness and success.

This is the story of gain and loss in this world. This worldly greatness is in itself a very great success, but if we compare it with success in the Hereafter, it is very insignificant. The real gain and loss is that of the Hereafter. There lies the true gain and loss, because that is the long life, the life that remains forever, the world that lasts forever. The real profit and real loss are there: Paradise, the gain of Allah's pleasure, or Hell, the loss of incurring Allah's displeasure. In the Hereafter, man will either have reached his highest progress and perfection, or will have so squandered himself that he will have lost his humanity. He will fall to the value of a stone, and will be less than a stone in comfort and ease.

﴿On the Day when a person will see what his hands have sent forth, and the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust!"﴾ (78:40).

The truth is that this surah shows a decisive and unambiguous path of truth; it tells us that all paths are paths of loss, except:

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and urge one another to truth, and urge one another to patience﴾ (103:3). And this is one path only, in which there is no multiplicity; it is the path of faith and righteous action. It is the path of establishing an Islamic community. The path of a community that counsels truth and urges goodness, whose provision is truthfulness and whose reward is patience.

The truth is that the path is one. This is why, whenever two Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met one another, they would not part until they had recited Surat al-'Asr. After that they would greet each other with salam and depart. In reality they were making a mutual pledge to follow this revolutionary constitution; they pledged to each other that they would remain on the path of righteousness of faith, that they would keep counseling truth and urging patience. And they pledged that they would be guardians of this constitution and remain members of the community that walks upon this constitution.
